findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so the block is trivially bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Emails elsewhere in the codebase are matched case-insensitively (e.g., User.find_by_username_or_email uses Email.downcase). A user can register as 'Spammer@Bad.com' and bypass a blocklist row stored as 'spammer@bad.com', defeating the entire purpose of this feature. The email should be normalized (downcased/stripped) before the lookup, and the blocked_emails.email uniqueness validation/index should be case-insensitive to match.

findings.title: match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write, losing counts under concurrency
findings.body: should_block? updates statistics with `record.match_count += 1; record.save`, which is a Ruby-side read-modify-write followed by a full-row save. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same match_count and one increment will be lost. Since this method runs on every validation of a User with a changed email, it is called from concurrent web requests routinely. The increment should be atomic in SQL (e.g., `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`) rather than a model save that also re-runs validations.

findings.title: User is validated twice in create, double-counting blocked-email match statistics
findings.body: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the new email validation, and the email validation now has a side effect: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and updates last_match_at on every invocation. Every blocked signup attempt therefore inflates match_count by 2 and issues an extra write, corrupting the tracking data the BlockedEmail model exists to collect. The counter update should be idempotent per attempt or moved out of the validation path.

findings.title: Any server-side email error permanently marks the address as 'invalid' in the client
findings.body: In createAccount, `result.errors.email` is true for every email error the server can return — including 'email already in use' (uniqueness) and 'not allowed from that email provider' (domain restrictions) — but the code unconditionally pushes the address into rejectedEmails, which makes emailValidation show the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' message for it. A user whose email was merely already registered, or whose domain was rejected, is told the address is syntactically invalid, and cannot resubmit it even after the underlying condition changes. The client should only blacklist the email when the error is the specific blocked-email failure, or surface the server's actual error message.

findings.title: action_type is NOT NULL with no database default, breaking the documented manual-load workflow
findings.body: The blocked_emails table is created with `t.integer :action_type, null: false` and no default. The BlockedEmail spec comment states the intended workflow is to 'manually load the table with some emails', i.e., admins inserting rows directly via SQL. Any INSERT that omits action_type (the natural thing when bulk-loading a list of addresses) will fail with a NOT NULL violation. A database default of 1 (the :block action value set by the model's set_defaults callback) would make manual loads work.

findings.title: No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator, and BlockedEmail is only ever stubbed
findings.body: EmailValidator now owns the email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic that was previously in User, but the new spec only exercises the BlockedEmail path with `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)`. There are no tests for the domain-restriction branches, for the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard that skips the blocked check when a restriction error was already added, nor any integration spec that the validator is actually wired onto User via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. A regression in any of these (including the conditional not firing when the email is unchanged) would go undetected. There is also no controller spec for the new `errors`/`values` fields in the create response that the JavaScript depends on.
